transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?
I've been making a lot of careless mistakes at work lately because I just can't seem to pay attention to details. It's getting really frustrating because I keep missing things that should be obvious.
Have these difficulties with attention and making careless mistakes been a recent change for you, or is this something you've struggled with since childhood?

It's been particularly bad for the last 11 months, which is why I'm finally seeking help. But honestly, I've struggled with making careless mistakes and paying attention since I was a kid, definitely before I turned 12. It's always been an issue for me, but it's just gotten overwhelming recently.
Along with focus issues, do you often feel restless, fidgety, or find yourself acting on impulse, both now and when you were younger?

Yes, I constantly feel restless and find myself fidgeting, like tapping my hands and feet all the time. I also tend to act impulsively, like blurting out answers before people even finish their questions. Just like the focus issues, I've had these restless and impulsive habits since I was a little kid.
Over the last 11 months, have you also been experiencing a persistently low or depressed mood, or a loss of interest in activities you usually enjoy?
No, I haven't really experienced a persistently low mood or lost interest in the things I enjoy doing. My mood is usually fine, it's just the frustration from my focus issues that gets to me.
Besides the frustration with your focus, have you been experiencing excessive, hard-to-control worry about various everyday things like work, health, or family over the last several months?

No, I don't really experience that kind of excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday things like my health or family. I definitely get stressed when I make mistakes at work, but it's not a constant, overwhelming anxiety about life in general.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Based on the patient's explicit denial of excessive, hard-to-control worry about everyday life events, Generalized Anxiety Disorder has been ruled out. The patient meets full criteria for ADHD, Combined Presentation, with both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms persisting since childhood (before age 12) and causing impairment. Therefore, the final diagnosis is Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation).
